speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: The GIC Portfolio has a more diversified asset composition, as well as a lower exposure to developed market, or DM (Developed Market) equities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: In addition, increasingly stretched valuations in DM equities have prompted a reduced allocation to this asset class in the GIC Portfolio in recent years.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: This has resulted in lower returns compared to the Reference Portfolio over the five-year period, as DM equities, especially those in the US, have done particularly well.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: However, we believe the high valuations of DM equities portend lower future returns." This was explained in the GIC Annual Report.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: All else being equal, a fund of a higher risk profile should generate higher returns over time, but the outcomes will be more volatile.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: As another example, a fund that is purely invested in publicly-listed equities and bonds would likely incur lower expenses than a fund that invests in real estate and private equity, as these are markets which are harder to access, but have the potential to yield further returns.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Minister for Finance)
text: Therefore, the Government's approach is not to apply a single benchmark, as my colleague Senior Minister of State Indranee Rajah had explained in a reply to another Parliamentary Question in July 2017 on a related matter.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Because even if one takes the view that these developed market equities might not hold good long-term returns, one could still have executed a strategy whereby this asset class was used to generate short-term returns before taking profit and exiting over the past five years.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My third supplementary question is really about benchmarking of performance.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In response to what the Minister said, I would like to ask: why the fact that the different Sovereign Wealth Funds may have different risk profiles and so on is the reason for not benchmarking performance against them?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One can still compare one's performance against other Sovereign Wealth Funds, even if they have different strategies, different risk profiles, for the sake of referencing the performance and referencing the strategy as well.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The fourth question: if such benchmarking is not being done against other Sovereign Wealth Funds, how does the Government derive an understanding of what is a good return and a good performance versus one that is less than good?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: First, under what conditions will the Government intervene?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Of course, if, on a continuous basis, there is under-performance by GIC, then certainly MOF and the Government will have to review fundamentally what has gone wrong and whether the strategies that GIC has undertaken are, indeed, the right ones.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On DM equities, I think it is easy to judge the reduced weightage by GIC on DM equities on hindsight and say that, "Look, they could have easily kept the weightage on DM equities over the last five years and rode the wave", but this is looking back on hindsight.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think the assessment by most market players and investment entities are that DM equities are, indeed, high in valuation and there is considerable uncertainty in DM equities today.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: One can take a short-term view, of course, and say, "Let's play the short-term game", but GIC is not a short-term player.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: GIC invests in the long-term and, in situations where there is market exuberance like now, GIC correctly, we think, takes a view that is more conservative and reduces its weightage on DM equities accordingly.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On benchmarking, that is really a function of risk and return.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As I have said earlier, the higher the risk, then, potentially, the higher returns one gets.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The Government has already set a Reference Portfolio which expresses the risk that we are prepared to take and GIC is allocated that risk budget and has to perform and achieve maximum returns according to that risk budget that it is accorded.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, the way we can easily evaluate GIC's performance is by looking at what is the amount of risk it takes and whether the returns it is getting are commensurate with the risk that it is undertaking in its portfolio.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is the benchmark or evaluation that we have put in place for GIC's investment strategies.
